findings.text: Start with a pending AfterFunc timer whose C field is nil (lines 173–178). If Stop cancels it before expiration, Stop returns true and that schedule will not call f. A second Stop without an intervening Reset returns false. If expiration wins instead, Stop also returns false, and the expiration path launches a goroutine for f (lines 66–75 and 181–182). Stop leaves the same Timer in place and does not wait for f to finish. The false result therefore cannot distinguish a previously canceled call from one launched by expiration. Launching the goroutine also does not establish that it has entered f.
findings.question: OPEN: Should the AfterFunc-specific wording qualify its claim that f has started to exclude repeated Stop calls after successful cancellation, and clarify that goroutine launch does not imply entry into f?

findings.text: Start with an initialized AfterFunc timer. Reset while it is active returns true and moves the pending execution to the new deadline. If a successful Stop or expiration came first, Reset returns false and schedules f on the same Timer. After cancellation there is no prior execution from that canceled schedule. After expiration, the prior execution may still be pending in its goroutine or running, and the new execution may overlap it. Reset preserves the Timer pointer and its nil C field and returns without waiting for either execution (lines 117–128, 138–144, and 173–182).

findings.text: Start with a running NewTimer whose channel has not yet been received from. Under the documented Go 1.23 behavior, Stop returns true and a receive after it returns blocks until the timer is rearmed and delivers a value. A repeated Stop before rearming returns false. Reset on a running timer under the same no-receive condition returns true. Reset after Stop or expiration returns false and still rearms the same Timer. A receive after Reset returns cannot get a value from the old settings under the Go 1.23 contract (lines 66–89 and 117–144). Before Go 1.23 a buffered value could survive either call and require an explicit drain. The constructor allocates a capacity-one channel, passes its pointer to the runtime, and exposes that same channel as C (lines 104–114).
findings.question: OPEN: What runtime mechanism presents the capacity-one allocation as a synchronous channel, and can configuration or module version select legacy buffering and stale-value behavior? The runtime implementation is absent from the excerpt.

findings.text: Start with a channel timer whose send callback is invoked after the intended send time. The callback samples Now, subtracts the supplied delta, and attempts one send without blocking (lines 146–156). If the send can proceed, the delivered value is the adjusted time. Otherwise the callback takes the default branch and returns without sending. After returns the channel of a newly created NewTimer and uses the same delivery path (lines 159–171). Both APIs document that as of Go 1.23 an unreferenced, unstopped timer can be collected before expiration (lines 95–102 and 163–168).
findings.question: OPEN: Under which channel modes and receive orderings can the runtime let the callback take its default branch, and does it ever retry delivery? The runtime delivery logic is absent from the excerpt.

findings.text: Start with a non-nil zero-value Timer, or another Timer whose initTimer is false. Stop panics with "time: Stop called on uninitialized Timer" before calling stopTimer. Reset panics with "time: Reset called on uninitialized Timer" before computing a deadline or calling resetTimer. Neither call returns a boolean or changes the Timer. Assigning C alone does not satisfy the guard (lines 60–64, 85–90, and 138–144).

findings.text: When NewTimer, AfterFunc, or Reset on an initialized Timer computes a deadline, a zero or negative duration gives the current runtimeNano value. A positive duration is added to that value, and a negative sum is clamped to MaxInt64. The caller then passes the deadline and a zero period to the runtime (lines 24–34, 110–114, 138–144, and 177–178). For AfterFunc, a deadline of now still goes through newTimer and the callback launches f in a separate goroutine. The excerpt does not establish whether f can begin before AfterFunc returns (lines 173–182). Sleep separately documents immediate return for nonpositive durations (lines 11–13).
